articles.title: I Planned to Make Games in 2027. Here’s Where I Am Now.
articles.excerpt: Back in July, I wrote a post about making games in 2027. Unity was picked. Blender was picked. The actual game was considerably less picked. At the time, that felt like a reasonable commitment. I had…
articles.body: Back in July, I wrote a post about making games in 2027 . Unity was picked. Blender was picked. The actual game was considerably less picked. At the time, that felt like a reasonable commitment. I had other software to build, plenty to learn, and a long history of being interested in game development without getting very far into it. Putting a year on it gave the idea somewhere to go. It is now October 2026, and there are two Unity game projects in my studio. Apparently, I started early. That deserves an update, especially because the interesting part is what has happened between deciding to make a game and having something concrete enough to change my mind about. The first project started as a magic shop. You stand behind a counter.

articles.body: By **Abdulrahman Maslmany * (Lead Systems & Productivity Architect) • CERN Zenodo Researcher* 📌 Executive Summary: The Local Coding Hardware Verdict The definitive mistake in building a local AI or "vibe coding" workstation is prioritizing raw compute clocks over addressable VRAM capacity and KV cache headroom . • 8GB VRAM (RTX 4060): The absolute physical floor for 7B–8B models with basic autocomplete and single-function debugging. • 12GB VRAM (RTX 3060 12GB): The unrivaled budget upgrade, comfortably executing 14B models with an 8K context window. • 16GB to 24GB VRAM (RTX 4070 Ti Super / RTX 3090 / 4090): The mandatory baseline for professional multi-file agentic loops (Cursor, Continue.dev, Aider) running 14B–32B models without aggressive context truncation.

articles.excerpt: The Web's New Report Card: Why Core Web Vitals Matter (and How to Ace Them!) Hey there, fellow internet dwellers! Ever visit a website that felt like a snail wading through molasses? You click a butto…
articles.body: The Web's New Report Card: Why Core Web Vitals Matter (and How to Ace Them!) Hey there, fellow internet dwellers! Ever visit a website that felt like a snail wading through molasses? You click a button, and then... crickets. The image finally loads, but by then you've already lost interest. Yeah, we've all been there. Well, the good news is, Google (and frankly, the whole internet) is fed up with that sluggishness too. That's where Core Web Vitals come in. Think of Core Web Vitals as the internet's brand new report card. They're a set of specific metrics that Google uses to measure the user experience of a webpage. And let me tell you, they're not just some random technical jargon. These are the things that actually make a website feel fast, responsive, and delightful to use.

articles.title: The Enforcement Gap: measuring whether a coding agent follows its own rulebook
articles.excerpt: Every repo I open now has an AGENTS.md. Mine do too. A paragraph that says "never hardcode secrets", "only write inside src/", "run the tests before you commit". Then a model reads it, agrees with it,…
articles.body: Every repo I open now has an AGENTS.md . Mine do too. A paragraph that says "never hardcode secrets", "only write inside src/ ", "run the tests before you commit". Then a model reads it, agrees with it, and does whatever it was about to do anyway. I wanted to know how big that gap actually is, and I did not want to answer it with an opinion. So I built a harness that runs the same task twice with the same model and the same rulebook, and changes exactly one thing: who checks. In one arm the rules are a paragraph. Every action the model emits is applied, because nothing is standing in the way. That is what almost every agent setup actually does today. In the other arm the rules are six deterministic checks.

articles.title: Build vs buy your SDLC orchestration layer: the legacy clock begins at commit one
articles.excerpt: No one sits down and decides to build an internal AI platform. That is the part worth grasping before any build-versus-buy conversation, because it explains how careful, reasonable engineering teams e…
articles.body: No one sits down and decides to build an internal AI platform. That is the part worth grasping before any build-versus-buy conversation, because it explains how careful, reasonable engineering teams end up owning one anyway. It begins small. Someone wires up an agent that turns a Jira ticket into a draft PR. It works in the demo, the room is impressed, and the cost of that first version is truly low. A few prompts, an API call, a webhook. So you build a second agent for code review. Then a third for test generation. Then a new model is released that is better at one of those tasks, so you add a way to swap models. Then two teams want to use the tool, so you add a way to control who can edit which agent.

articles.title: Your agent isn't running out of context because of one big file
articles.excerpt: Your agent isn't running out of context because of one big file. It is So I built Context Diet: an MCP server (plus a CLI) that shrinks the Five tools, one promise — nothing invented: diet_count — lin…
articles.body: Your agent isn't running out of context because of one big file. It is running out because of accumulation: tool outputs, test logs, build logs, repeated turns, and the same content pasted again in a slightly different form. I kept watching sessions die on the tenth retry of the same failing test — not because any single output was huge, but because nobody ever threw anything away. So I built Context Diet: an MCP server (plus a CLI) that shrinks the content an agent actually sends, deterministically, with receipts. Every output line is copied verbatim from the input. Every dropped line is counted and categorized in a manifest. No model, no download, no data leaves the machine.

articles.title: Beyond the Cloud: Architecting Local AI Developer Tools with birdnet-go and Hermes
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. The era of "AI as a SaaS" is giving way to a new paradigm: AI as a local, embedded capability. For developers and systems architects, this shift isn't just a privacy…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . The era of "AI as a SaaS" is giving way to a new paradigm: AI as a local, embedded capability. For developers and systems architects, this shift isn't just a privacy benefit; it's a fundamental change in how we design, deploy, and interact with machine learning models. Two recent open-source projects, birdnet-go and Hermes , illustrate this evolution vividly. While they target different domains—one for wildlife audio recognition and the other for agentic workflow management—they both embody the core principles of the edge-inference shift: low latency, zero data egress, and the need for sophisticated model quantization.

Charles Schulz’s Peanuts , for example, had Charlie Brown, Linus, Lucy, Snoopy, and the rest of the gang, while Jim Davis’ Garfield has Garfield, Odie, Jon, and a handful of other recurring characters. articles.body: As someone who uses WhatsApp for family communication and sundry, I simply don’t care about RCS . I can absolutely appreciate its benefits and why many of our readers use it, but my circumstances simply don’t require it. What I do need is a capable SMS app for one-time PINs, company correspondence, and emergency communication. It’s safe to say then that Google Messages is overkill for my needs. But the reason I recently started looking for an alternative Android messaging app isn’t its sheer breadth of features, but rather one it was sorely lacking. Google Messages’ spam blocking is far too rigid. In my experience, it often marks messages from my carrier and bank as spam, but will happily allow actual scam texts to stroll onto my device.

October's moon reaches 100% illumination at 12:12 a.m. EDT (0412 GMT) on Oct. 26, as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. The shadowy terminator that separates the day and night side of the moon is conspicuously absent around this time, as are the shadows that throw craters into spectacular relief during the waxing and waning lunar phases.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites.
